newsitem.title: USA: FCC chief doubts high court will reinstate phone rules.
newsitem.headline: FCC chief doubts high court will reinstate phone rules.

text.p: The chairman of the Federal Communications Commission said Friday it was "a long shot" the Supreme Court would reinstate landmark FCC rules designed to break open the nation's local phone monopolies.
The chairman, Reed Hundt, said it was unlikely the rules would be put into effect for at least 1-1/2 years, if ever, while they are fought over in the courts.
In the meantime, he said, the FCC "must count on" state regulators to voluntarily adopt the FCC's suspended policies for opening the $100 billion local phone market.

The Supreme Court is considering a request by the FCC and long-distance carriers such as AT&T Corp. and MCI Communications Corp. to reactivate the rules after a federal appeals court in St. Louis supended key provisions of the FCC's "interconnection" order.

The order spells out how long-distance carriers, cable-TV operators and others can link up to the local phone network under the new telecommunications law. The Eight Circuit appeals court "stayed" pricing and other provisions while it considers a court challenge to the order.
"It's pretty much of a long shot that the Supreme Court will lift the stay or that the Eighth Circuit will change its mind on that issue," Hundt told a news conference.

At the end of last month, Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas refused to lift the stay after the FCC and the long-distance carriers asked him to do so. Thomas oversees appeals from the Eighth Circuit.
His action was a victory for the Baby Bell phone companies, other local carriers and state regulators seeking to overturn the interconnection order.
Hundt said it was unlikely the suspended provisions would be put back into effect for a while.

"Our mandate has been set aside and I would not expect that it was likely that it would be put back into effect unless, and until, the Supreme Court reversed the Eighth Circuit, which I don't think is likely to be decided any earlier than the Spring of 1998," he said.
